answers.text: I'm a test analyst at an IT services firm in Chennai, with about two years of experience. I started with regression testing on a card-statement portal, and then moved to a banking client's loan module. In the first year I logged 210 defects. Later I wrote test plans for two releases, which is a step beyond running test cases. I now want an MBA because I understand how the software fails, but I don't understand how the bank decides what to build.

My role involves working with multiple stakeholders in a fast-paced environment to ensure quality deliverables. I take ownership and drive results, and I believe I add value to the team and the organisation.

The test-planning work for the two releases was my biggest responsibility. I listed the risky loan flows first, such as interest calculation and part-payments, and tested those before the screens. Two of my defects there were marked critical by the developers.
As the owner of the test plans, I also had four testers reporting to me and I did their appraisals. That is the part of the job I am proudest of.
I can't tell you the client's name or the loan volumes. Our contract with them is confidential, so I can only describe my own testing tasks.
I don't know what percentage of our defects were fixed before release. The developers tracked that and I never saw the final report.
I don't agree that testing is a purely technical role. Writing test plans needs judgement about business risk. So I would not say I have no business exposure.
Just to share, I am also trying to learn to bake sourdough bread at home. My first loaf was very hard, but the second one was better.
